subject: writing a simple for-loop to find the high tide

messages.author: 1ec981f6ad974842
messages.subject: writing a simple for-loop to find the high tide
parts:
Hey y'all,

I'm trying to write a for-loop that finds the high tide in a vector of 10-minute tide recordings.  When it finds the high tide, I'd like it to spit that value into a new vector.  I generated some simple sample data (attached) that simulates the dataset with integers.  So far, I have:

d <- read.csv("numbers.csv", header=T)

m=0

for (i in 1:length(d$numbers)) {

if(d$numbers[i]>=m) {d$numbers[i] -> m} 

else {m=m}

}

This successfully spits out the first "high tide" value (8), but I don't know how to make it keep going through the whole vector to get the next two values (which should be 5 and 8, respectively).  

Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Best,
Myfanwy

--

parts:
Hi Myfanwy, 

This is a slightly different logical approach, but it will create a vector of  c( 8, 5, 8) as you suggest:
d <- read.csv("numbers.csv", header=T)

highs = NA
j=1
for (i in 2:(length(d$numbers)-1))
  {
    if(d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i-1] & d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i+1])
       {highs[j] <- d$numbers[i] ; j = j+1} 
  }




However, I wonder if you also don't want a way to extract the row in which the high tides occur? Here is the same code with a few extra lines to pull that information as well and put it all into one dataframe:
d <- read.csv("numbers.csv", header=T)

highs = data.frame(tide.height = rep(NA,10), tide.row = rep(NA,10))
j=1
for (i in 2:(length(d$numbers)-1))
  {
    if(d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i-1] & d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i+1])
         { highs$tide.height[j] <- d$numbers[i] 
           highs$tide.row[j] <- as.numeric(rownames(d)[i])
           j = j+1} 
  }
highs = highs[!is.na(highs$tide.height),]


The 'rep(NA,10)' at the top and the matching line at the bottom to remove extra NAs is a bit messy, plus the value of 10 would potentially have to be increased for larger datasets. If anyone has better code to clean that up, please do!  


- Anna

messages.author: 8c8f0ca54c4a2459
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: writing a simple for-loop to find the high tide
parts:
Myfanwy,

pastecs::turnpoints does exactly this:

library(pastecs)
data = read.csv("numbers.csv")
turn = turnpoints(data$numbers)
hightides = data$numbers[turn$peaks]
hightides

[1] 8 5 8

The object turn$peaks is a logical vectors with TRUE in any position which is a peak in your vector. turn also has turn$pits and a lot of other diagnostic data.

Another solution, suggested by Ben Bolker on StackOverflow here is

turn2 = which(diff(sign(diff(data$numbers)))==-2)+1
data$numbers[turn$peaks]

diff-sign-siff here gets the differences between each consecutive number, and checks when these differences change sign from positive to negative (1 to -1 as returned by sign). If you change the -2 to 2, you’ll get the pits instead of the peaks. The +1 at the end deals with the fact that diff returns a result ` shorter than the original.

If your data are noisy Tim Poisot has a solution here: http://rtricks.wordpress.com/2009/05/03/an-algorithm-to-find-local-extrema-in-a-vector/, and the discussion to StackOverflow above has some discussion of options.

Noam

d <- read.csv("numbers.csv", header=T)

m=0
high=NULL

for (i in 1:length(d$numbers)) {

if(d$numbers[i]>=m) {d$numbers[i] -> m}

else {

c(high, m)
m <- 0

next

}

}

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: writing a simple for-loop to find the high tide
parts: turnpoints is robust to repeated maxima, but the diff-sign-diff solution is not. With repeats at the peaks, turnpoints$peaks will return TRUE values at the FIRST of the repeated peak values. diff-sign-diff will miss it altogether.
